35 An ideal diode has zero resistance when forward biased and infinite resistance when reverse
biased. The diode is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor across the terminals of a source
having electromotive force (e.m.f.) 3 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, as shown.
2 Ω
3 V
1 Ω
V
diode
A high-resistance voltmeter is connected across the diode and resistor.
Which row gives the readings of the voltmeter for the two ways of connecting the diode?
reverse
forward
biased
biased
A
1 V
3 V
B
2 V
0 V
C
2 V
3 V

3 V
0 V

hints: Notice the high-resistance voltmeter is connected across the series combination of the $2 \, \Omega$ resistor and the diode, so it reads the terminal p.d. of the $3 \, \text{V}$ source.
Recall the ideal diode rules given: $0 \, \Omega$ when forward biased so current can flow, and infinite resistance when reverse biased so the branch is an open circuit.
Connect this to $E = I(R+r)$ and $V = E - Ir$: calculate $I$ with $2 \, \Omega + 1 \, \Omega$ for forward bias, and set $I = 0$ for reverse bias.
walkthrough: Identify the circuit: e.m.f. $E = 3 \, \text{V}$ with internal $r = 1 \, \Omega$ in series with external $R = 2 \, \Omega$ plus the diode. The voltmeter reads $V$ across the external $2 \, \Omega$ plus diode.
Forward biased: diode resistance $= 0 \, \Omega$. Total circuit resistance is $R + r = 2 \, \Omega + 1 \, \Omega = 3 \, \Omega$.

Current is $I = E/(R+r) = 3 \, \text{V} / 3 \, \Omega = 1 \, \text{A}$. Terminal p.d. is $V = E - Ir = 3 \, \text{V} - (1 \, \text{A})(1 \, \Omega) = 2 \, \text{V}$, which also equals $I \times 2 \, \Omega$.
Reverse biased: diode resistance is infinite, so the series branch is open and $I = 0 \, \text{A}$. Lost volts $Ir = 0 \, \text{V}$.
With no current the voltmeter, which draws negligible current, reads the full e.m.f.: $V = E = 3 \, \text{V}$. Forward $2 \, \text{V}$ and reverse $3 \, \text{V}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: 1 V is the drop across the $1 \, \Omega$ internal resistance when forward biased, not the terminal p.d. across the $2 \, \Omega$ resistor and diode.

B.explanation: 2 V is correct for forward bias, but 0 V is wrong for reverse bias because with zero current there is no lost volts and the voltmeter reads the full $3 \, \text{V}$ e.m.f.

C.explanation: Forward bias gives $2 \, \text{V}$ terminal p.d. with $1 \, \text{A}$ current, and reverse bias gives $3 \, \text{V}$ with zero current and zero lost volts.

D.explanation: 3 V is wrong for forward bias because some $3 \, \text{V}$ e.m.f. is lost across the $1 \, \Omega$ internal resistance when $1 \, \text{A}$ flows.
